cases.title: Two hours free, wants to do two days in one
cases.situation: Gabe, 32, lifting 2 years, upper/lower 4 days a week, full gym, nothing hurts. He missed Wednesday's lower day (squat 4 × 5 at 245, Romanian deadlift, lunges, leg curl). Today, Thursday, is upper. He types: "I'll just do both today, Wednesday's then Thursday's. I've got two hours."
cases.short: Same as today: no stacking. Do Wednesday's lower day today and slide the week a day. If he can't slide, squat 4 × 5 at 245 first, then the upper day, and drop the other leg work.
cases.today: Never stack missed sessions into one day. One missed workout pushes the week back a day if the schedule allows. Otherwise its main lift folds into the next session and its accessories are dropped.
cases.rec: Same as today; the rule is fine. Today becomes Wednesday's lower day in full, and upper moves to tomorrow with the rest of the week one day later. If he can't train an extra day: squat 4 × 5 at 245 first, then Thursday's upper day as written; Romanian deadlift, lunges and leg curl are dropped with nothing to make up. Stacking is not one of the safety rules, so if he still says he wants both, the coach lets him: lower day first, stop each set at the planned effort, and no weight goes up off the lifts done late in the session.
cases.why: A 2012 review of exercise order found that lifts placed late in a session get fewer total reps across their sets, whatever the muscle, and that people gained less strength on the lifts done last. A 2021 review on training when short of time found the week's total sets matter more than which day they fall on, so sliding a day costs nothing. I found no trial of two full sessions done back to back. Coaching judgment.

sources.t: Exercise Order in Resistance Training (Simão, de Salles, Figueiredo, Dias, Willardson, Sports Medicine, 2012; abstract read on a university record)
No Time to Lift? Designing Time-Efficient Training Programs for Strength and Hypertrophy: A Narrative Review (Iversen, Norum, Schoenfeld, Fimland, Sports Medicine, 2021)

cases.reply: Let's not stack them. Do Wednesday's lower day today, squats at 245 for 4 × 5 and the rest as written, then upper tomorrow, and the week slides one day. If tomorrow's out, do the squats first today, then your upper day, and skip the other leg work. Nothing to make up either way.

cases.title: The next dumbbells are a 25% jump
cases.situation: Lena, 28, lifting 1 year, wants muscle, full gym, nothing hurts. Dumbbell shoulder press with 20s, range 8 to 12: she got 12, 12, 11 at effort 8 out of 10. Her gym's dumbbells go from 20 to 25 lb, a 25% jump. Last month she tried the 25s and got 5, 4, 4.
cases.short: Ask about 22.5s or add-on weights first. If there are none: build the 20s to 3 sets of 15, then switch one set at a time to the 25s, counting 5 or more reps as a good set for the first few weeks.
cases.today: Today's 12, 12, 11 is in the range but not at the top, so same weight and chase reps. Once every set is 12, the jump the app wants (about 1 lb) is smaller than one dumbbell step, so it adds a rep per set: 13s, then 14s. At 14s it takes the 25s anyway and asks for 8. The 10% limit doesn't stop that step. By the app's own rep math, 14 reps with 20s is about 5 with 25s, so she would miss 8 twice and be reset to the 20s.
cases.rec: First ask if the gym has 22.5s, clip-on add-on weights (1.25 or 2.5 lb), or a shoulder press machine with smaller steps; if so, use them. If not, when the next step is more than 10% heavier: keep adding a rep per set on the 20s up to 3 sets of 15. Then set 1 with the 25s for as many as she can at effort 8 (expect 5 to 7) and sets 2 and 3 with the 20s. Move a set to the 25s each time the 25 sets reach 8. Reps of 5 or more on the 25s don't count as a miss during the switch. Slower lowering on the 20s is fine as an extra, not as the plan.
cases.why: A 2021 review of loading (Schoenfeld and others) found muscle grows about the same across a wide range of weights and reps as long as sets are hard, so more weeks at 13 to 15 reps cost her nothing. NASM's coaching guide suggests upper-body jumps of about 2 to 5%. I found no study of this exact switch. The app math is my own check. Coaching judgment.

sources.t: Loading Recommendations for Muscle Strength, Hypertrophy, and Local Endurance: A Re-Examination of the Repetition Continuum (Schoenfeld, Grgic, Van Every, Plotkin, Sports, 2021)
Progressive Overload Explained: Programming Progress for Every Client (Andre Adams, NASM, 2021)

cases.reply: Stay with the 20s and add a rep to each set: 12s, then 13s, up to 15s. Does your gym have 22.5s or small clip-on weights? If not, once you reach 15s your first set moves to the 25s, where 5 to 7 reps is right on track, and the other two sets stay on the 20s.

cases.title: "Is the trap bar cheating?"
cases.situation: Owen, 45, lifting 1 year, general strength, full gym with a trap bar, nothing hurts. His plan has barbell deadlift 3 × 5 at 185. He watched a friend hurt his back deadlifting and types: "I don't want to do barbell deadlifts. Is the trap bar cheating?"
cases.short: Not cheating. Make the trap-bar deadlift his main pulling-from-the-floor lift and don't bring the barbell deadlift back unless he asks or his goal changes to one that needs it.
cases.today: Lifts an athlete dislikes are swapped for an equivalent, and the trap-bar deadlift is in the exercise list (offered when a trap bar is ticked in his equipment). After repeated swaps the app asks whether to stop suggesting the lift. In the list the trap-bar deadlift is an accessory, not a main lift. The rules don't say whether the coach should ever raise the barbell deadlift again.
cases.rec: Swap to the trap-bar deadlift and treat it as his main lift for that slot: same sets, reps and progression. Say plainly it is a real deadlift. Keep Romanian deadlifts or leg curls in the week, because the trap bar works the thighs more and the hamstrings and lower back a little less. For a general-strength goal the coach never pushes the barbell deadlift again. It comes up once only if he asks, or if he picks a goal that needs a straight bar, such as a powerlifting meet.
cases.why: Swinton 2011 (19 powerlifters): the trap bar lowered the peak load at the lower back and hip, raised it at the knee, and they lifted more with it. Camara 2016 (20 trained men): more thigh activity, less hamstring and lower-back activity, same max. An NSCA trainers' journal article (2026) says near-max barbell deadlifts aren't needed outside powerlifting. All single-session lab studies on men; no long-term injury comparison found. Mixed evidence.

sources.t: A biomechanical analysis of straight and hexagonal barbell deadlifts using submaximal loads (Swinton and others, Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 2011; abstract read)

An Examination of Muscle Activation and Power Characteristics While Performing the Deadlift Exercise with Straight and Hexagonal Barbells (Camara, Coburn, Dunnick, Brown, Galpin, Costa, Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 2016)
Rethinking Heavy Barbell Training: Injury Risk vs. Necessity in Non-Powerlifting Populations (Nick Tumminello, NSCA Personal Training Quarterly, 2026)

cases.reply: Not cheating. The trap-bar deadlift is a real deadlift, and I've swapped it in as your main one, starting at 185 for 3 sets of 5. Your Romanian deadlifts stay in for the hamstrings. If you ever want the barbell back, just say so.

cases.title: Week two and wants to find her one-rep max
cases.situation: Zoe, 24, in her second week, general fitness, full gym, nothing hurts. Her last squat session was 65 × 8, 8, 8 at effort 7 out of 10. She types: "My friend squats 135. I want to find my one-rep max this week so I know where I am."
cases.short: No true max yet. Give her the estimate from her own sets now (about 85 to 90), offer a hard set of 3 to 5 in week 4, and a real max test after about 8 to 12 weeks of clean squatting.
cases.today: The first two sessions of a new lift are for finding the weight. Beginners work at efforts 6 to 8 out of 10. The app estimates a max from logged sets and shows it. The rules on testing a max are written for athletes with a dated event and don't mention beginners.
cases.rec: Don't test a true max in the first weeks. Give her the number she is asking for from her logged sets (65 × 8 at effort 7 is about 85 to 90) and say it will be more accurate as she logs heavier sets. In week 4, offer one hard set of 3 to 5 reps at effort 8 to get a better estimate. A real one-rep test is fine once she has squatted for about 8 to 12 weeks, her last form review was clean, and she has safety bars or a spotter. Not for anyone training lighter for a health reason. If she pushes back now, offer the set of 3 to 5 this week, not a single.
cases.why: Sources disagree. A 2020 systematic review found one-rep max tests reliable and generally safe even in untrained people, with soreness the only common problem. ACE's trainer guidance says a true max is not appropriate for beginners and an estimate from reps is the better choice. A US military fitness page says rep-based estimates work well at 5 reps or fewer. So the wait is about learning the lift, not proven danger. Mixed evidence.

sources.t: Test-Retest Reliability of the One-Repetition Maximum (1RM) Strength Assessment: a Systematic Review (Grgic, Lazinica, Schoenfeld, Pedisic, Sports Medicine - Open, 2020)
Understanding 1-RM and Predicted 1-RM Assessments (Clarissa Jimenez, American Council on Exercise, 2018)
What is a one-rep max? (Human Performance Resources by CHAMP, 2022)

cases.reply: From your 65 × 8 last session, your max is about 85 to 90 right now, and that number will sharpen as you log heavier sets. Let's hold off on a true max for a few more weeks. In week 4 we'll do one hard set of 3 to 5 to pin it down, and a real max test after that.

cases.title: "Should I be wearing a belt?"
cases.situation: Hank, 40, lifting 12 years, squat 365 × 3, deadlift 455 × 2, full gym, nothing hurts. He types: "Should I be wearing a belt? When do I put it on?"
cases.short: Optional. If he wants one: heaviest squat and deadlift sets only, warm-ups without it, and never as a fix for a sore or tight back.
cases.rec: A belt is optional and he doesn't need one. If he wants it: put it on for the last warm-up and the top sets of squat and deadlift (for him, from about 315 on squat and 405 on deadlift), snug enough to push his stomach out against it, and off for everything else. He should be able to brace the same way without it first. A belt never changes the pain rules: a tight lower back still means no spinal loading that session. For anyone with a heart or blood pressure condition on file, no belt advice and no breath-holding cues, as today.
cases.why: Sources disagree. A sports doctor's 2023 review of the studies: belts raise pressure in the trunk in most studies, may help heavy sets move a little better, and haven't been shown to prevent back injury. A review written for the NSCA by a spine researcher (McGill, 2005) is more cautious: no protection for healthy people, a possible help only for very heavy lifting, never a stand-in for technique, and may raise blood pressure. I did not find the NSCA textbook's own wording. Mixed evidence.

sources.t: The Science of Weight Lifting Belts (Jordan Feigenbaum, MD, Barbell Medicine, 2023)
On The Use Weight Belts (Stuart McGill, review invited by the NSCA, 2005)
The Weight Belt Controversy (Frankel and Kravitz, University of New Mexico; year not shown)

cases.reply: It's optional, and you don't need one. If you want it, put it on for your last warm-up and top sets of squat and deadlift, around 315 and up on squat and 405 and up on deadlift, and leave it off for everything else. Take a big breath and push your stomach out against it. It's not a fix for a sore back, so tell me if that ever comes up.

cases.title: "Three months and I look exactly the same"
cases.situation: Maya, 36, three months in, 3 days a week, general fitness, full gym, nothing hurts. She has done 37 of 39 planned sessions. Her squat went from 65 × 8 to 115 × 8 and her body weight is unchanged. She types: "Three months and I look exactly the same. What's the point?"
cases.short: No pep talk and nothing about her body. Show her own numbers, give one next target (125 × 8), and offer one change if she wants it.
cases.today: The voice rules: short, direct, warm, no hype, and never comment on body shape. The rules don't cover what to say when an athlete is discouraged about how she looks.
cases.rec: One line that takes the frustration seriously, then her own numbers: 37 of 39 sessions, squat 65 × 8 to 115 × 8. One concrete next target: 125 × 8 within about three weeks. Then one offer, her choice: if size is what she wants, the plan can be rebuilt for muscle size. The coach says nothing about how she looks, doesn't promise a date for visible change, and doesn't argue her out of the feeling. If asked how long, it can say honestly that visible change usually trails strength by months.
cases.why: Cleveland Clinic's guide: strength shows up within about 3 to 4 weeks, small visible changes around 2 to 3 months, and clearer ones around 4 to 6 months, so she is early, not failing. On what keeps people going, the evidence is thin: one systematic review (in older adults) found feedback and progress tracking was the only approach linked to better exercise adherence, and its authors said the evidence was not enough to recommend it. Coaching judgment.

sources.t: How Long Does It Take To Build Muscle? (Cleveland Clinic, 2025)

What interventions are used to improve exercise adherence in older people and what behavioural techniques are they based on? A systematic review (Room, Hannink, Dawes, Barker, BMJ Open, 2017; abstract read on a university record)

cases.reply: That's frustrating, and I hear it. Here's what three months did: 37 of 39 sessions, and your squat went from 65 × 8 to 115 × 8. Next target is 125 × 8, about three weeks away at this pace. If building size is what you're after, I can rebuild the plan around that. Want me to?

cases.title: Seven drinks, five hours of sleep, squats at 9am
cases.situation: Tom, 30, 185 lb, lifting 4 years, full gym, nothing hurts. Saturday 9am session: squat 4 × 5 at 275. His check-in is red (5 hours of sleep, low energy). He types: "Rough night, about 7 drinks, 5 hours of sleep. Still lifting?"
cases.short: Ask one thing first: does he still feel the drinks? If yes, no lifting today, move it to Sunday. If no, a short, lighter session or move it, his choice.
cases.today: A red day is a shorter session or mobility only, with an offer to move the workout; a low yellow keeps the weights and takes a set off each exercise. The rules cover sleep and readiness but say nothing about alcohol.
cases.rec: No moralizing and no comment on the drinking. The coach asks once whether he still feels the drinks (unsteady, dizzy or queasy). If yes: no barbell work today, move the session to Sunday. That part is firm, even if he pushes back. If no: offer to move it, or a short session: squat 2 sets of 5 at about 250 (10% lighter), effort 7 out of 10 or below, water and food first, and no weight increase earned from today. If he feels clear and wants the planned 275, that is his call, as with any red day. This adds a safety rule; it loosens none.
cases.why: An NSCA coaches' article (2017): being intoxicated hurts balance, coordination and reaction time; a hangover brings fluid and blood sugar problems and poor sleep; one figure cited is about 11% off endurance, and the effect on strength is unclear. Barnes's 2014 review: about 0.5 g of alcohol per kg is unlikely to hurt recovery; 7 drinks is roughly double that for him. Parr 2014 found a larger dose after training lowered muscle rebuilding even with protein. No study of heavy lifting the morning after. Coaching judgment.

sources.t: The Effects of Alcohol on Athletic Performance (Claire Siekaniec, NSCA Coach, 2017)
Alcohol: Impact on Sports Performance and Recovery in Male Athletes (Barnes, Sports Medicine, 2014; abstract read)

Alcohol ingestion impairs maximal post-exercise rates of myofibrillar protein synthesis following a single bout of concurrent training (Parr and others, PLoS ONE, 2014; abstract read on a university record)

cases.reply: One question first: do you still feel the drinks at all, unsteady or queasy? If yes, no lifting today and we move it to tomorrow. If you're just tired, drink some water, eat, and do a short one: 2 sets of 5 at 250, nothing that grinds. Or we move it to tomorrow, your call.

cases.title: "Can I still grow on two days?"
cases.situation: Ana, 33, lifting 2 years, wants muscle size, full gym, nothing hurts. A new job leaves her 2 days a week, about 60 minutes each. She has been on 4 days. She types: "Can I still grow on two days?"
cases.short: Yes. Two full-body days, every muscle both days, aiming for about 8 to 10 hard sets per muscle a week, with pushes and pulls paired to fit 60 minutes.
cases.today: The guide says 2 days is full body A / B, each with a squat or lunge, a hinge, a push and a pull, and that a plan with few days can land under the weekly number (12 hard sets per muscle for her). Changing days is a rebuild. Reading the plan builder, the muscle-size plan is written for 4 to 5 days, so a 2-day athlete with that goal appears to get the 4-day upper/lower plan two days at a time: each muscle about once a week at about half the target. If it did build A / B, by my count chest and shoulders top out near 5 direct sets a week. I could not run it here; worth checking.
cases.rec: Tell her yes, and send her to Rebuild program for 2 days. The plan should be two full-body days that train every major muscle both days. The coach tunes the weekly number to 10, the bottom of her range, so the plan isn't chasing 12 it can't reach, and expects about 8 to 10 hard sets per muscle. To fit 60 minutes: 5 to 6 lifts a day, 3 to 4 sets, pushes and pulls done back to back, sets taken to effort 8 to 9 out of 10. Be honest that growth may be a little slower than on 4 days. If she gets a third day back, rebuild again.
cases.why: A 2016 meta-analysis (Schoenfeld and others) found training a muscle twice a week grew more than once a week; a 2019 review found that with equal weekly sets, how often matters little. A 2021 review puts the floor at about 4 hard sets per muscle a week and cites a pooled analysis where under 5, 5 to 9 and 10 or more sets gave about 5%, 7% and 10% growth. So two days works if each muscle is hit both days. Strong evidence; the code reading is mine and untested.

sources.t: Effects of Resistance Training Frequency on Measures of Muscle Hypertrophy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis (Schoenfeld, Ogborn, Krieger, Sports Medicine, 2016; abstract read)

Resistance training frequency and skeletal muscle hypertrophy: A review of available evidence (Grgic, Schoenfeld, Latella, Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport, 2019; abstract read on a university record)
No Time to Lift? Designing Time-Efficient Training Programs for Strength and Hypertrophy: A Narrative Review (Iversen, Norum, Schoenfeld, Fimland, Sports Medicine, 2021)

cases.reply: Yes, you can still grow on two days. Tap Rebuild program on the Progress tab and pick 2 days: you'll get two full-body sessions that hit every muscle both days, about 8 to 10 hard sets each per week. I'll pair your pushes and pulls so it fits in 60 minutes. Progress may be a little slower than on four days, but it keeps going.

cases.title: Bench press: the bar tilts and the left arm locks out late
cases.situation: Drew, 31, lifting 3 years, wants a 225 bench, full gym, nothing hurts. Bench press, 185 × 6, filmed from the front (camera at the foot of the bench). Reps 1 to 3: bar level, both arms finish together. Reps 4 to 6: on the way up the bar tilts with the right end about 2 inches higher, his left elbow flares out wide, both wrists bend back, and the left arm locks out about half a second after the right. No bounce, and his hips stay down.
cases.today: From the front the app scores three things: range (each rep against the deepest one), control on the way down, and whether the last rep slows compared with the first. Bar path and back angle aren't judged from this view. It does measure how far apart in height the two hands get on each rep (a tilted bar), but that number isn't part of the score. It doesn't measure elbow flare, wrist bend or which arm locks out first; the coach only sees those in the frames. There is no fault list yet, so nothing says which fault comes first, form faults don't change the weight, and a repeat fault adds no work.
cases.rec:
Fault: The bar tilting from rep 4 is the main one: the left side is running out first. The left elbow flaring and the late left lockout follow from it. Wrists bending back is a separate, smaller fault.
Cue: "Squeeze the bar, knuckles to the ceiling, push both hands up together." Setup check first: same finger on the ring marks on both sides, and lying centered on the bench.
Severity: Moderate. Major if it tilts from rep 1, or if the left shoulder goes from "a bit weaker" to hurting (then the pain rules apply as they do today).
Lower the weight: Yes, a little: 185 to 175 (about 5%) for the next two bench sessions, filmed front-on, and no move to 190 yet. A level bar on every rep earns 185 back. Smaller than the 10% in the overhead press case because reps 1 to 3 are clean, nothing bounces and nothing hurts. If it still tilts at 175 with an even grip, go to 165.
If it keeps happening: Dumbbell bench press as his second pressing lift, 3 sets of 8 to 12, with the left side setting the reps for both arms, plus face pulls or band pull-aparts. Drop them after 3 clean front-on reviews.
cases.why: Thin evidence. A 2024 modelling study of bench technique found sideways forces on the bar differ a lot between lifters and change the load on the shoulder, and that a grip no wider than 1.5 times shoulder width with the shoulder blades pulled back lowers shoulder load; its summary gave no result for elbow angle. A 2007 NSCA journal review says the same on grip width. The one review of training to even out side-to-side differences covered legs only and found small, uncertain effects from one-sided or two-sided work. Nothing solid on wrist position. The 5% drop follows the head coach's view that form breaking on late reps means the weight went up too fast. Coaching judgment.

sources.t: Effects of bench press technique variations on musculoskeletal shoulder loads and potential injury risk (Noteboom, Belli, Hoozemans, Seth, Veeger, van der Helm, Frontiers in Physiology, 2024; abstract read on a university record)
The affect of grip width on bench press performance and risk of injury (Green and Comfort, Strength and Conditioning Journal, 2007; abstract read on a university record)

The Effects of Training Interventions on Inter-Limb Asymmetries: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis (Bettariga, Turner, Maloney, Maestroni, Jarvis, Bishop; accepted copy on a university record, journal not shown)

cases.reply: Drew, reps 1 to 3 are level. From rep 4 your left side lags: the bar tilts about 2 inches and your left arm locks out late. Check that the same finger is on the ring on both sides, then squeeze the bar, knuckles to the ceiling, and push both hands up together. Next two bench sessions are at 175, filmed front-on; a level bar on every rep gets you back to 185.

cases.title: "110 is still a stretch. Is 90 enough?"
cases.situation: Carla, 38, lifting 1 year, wants to build muscle, 150 lb, nothing hurts. On Nov 25 her protein target was lowered from 120 g to 110 g. Over the four weeks since she has averaged about 90 g and hit 110 on 6 days of 28. Her weight is unchanged at 150 and she eats at maintenance. Squat went from 115 × 8 to 120 × 8; dumbbell press is flat. She types: "110 is still a stretch. Is 90 enough? I am getting a bit stronger."
cases.today: The app sets protein at about 0.8 g per lb (120 g for her) and the guide's range is 0.7 to 1.0 g per lb. The head coach's Nov 25 call, not in the rules yet, lowered her to 110 g, to be raised slowly if she doesn't see gains. Nothing says how long to wait, how big a step is, or what counts as no gains. Food changes follow the 2 to 3 week trend.
cases.rec: Keep the head coach's approach: a target she can hit, raised slowly. Answer her straight: 90 g is enough to keep getting a bit stronger and is on the low side for building muscle. Set the target at 100 g now (her usual day plus one protein food). A target counts as hit when she is within 5 g on 5 days of 7. Step: 10 g a day, only after two weeks of hitting the current target, up to 110 g and no higher. Review every 4 weeks. "No gains" means that over 4 weeks of on-plan training, half or more of her main lifts show no added weight or reps. Today is one up and one flat: slow, not none, so no forced raise. If she reaches 110 and lifts are still flat for 4 weeks, the next lever is food overall: offer 100 to 200 more calories a day, her choice. Food first: Greek yogurt at breakfast, her lightest meal, then an egg or lentil soup at lunch. No comment on her body and no food called good or bad. Open point for the reviewer: this lowers the Nov 25 target from 110 to 100.
cases.why: Morton's 2018 meta-analysis: muscle gain from lifting stopped improving above about 1.6 g per kg a day (110 g for her), and the extra muscle from added protein was modest, about 0.3 kg on average. The sports nutrition society's 2017 position stand gives 1.4 to 2.0 g per kg (95 to 136 g for her), about 20 to 40 g per meal every 3 to 4 hours, and says whole foods can cover it. So 90 g is just under the range and 100 g is inside it. Strong evidence on the amounts. The 4-week review, the 10 g step and the definition of no gains are coaching judgment, built on the plateau guide's 3-week rule.

sources.t: A systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression of the effect of protein supplementation on resistance training-induced gains in muscle mass and strength in healthy adults (Morton and others, British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2018; abstract read on a university record)
International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: Protein and Exercise (Jäger and others, Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, 2017; abstract read on a university record)

cases.reply: 90 is enough to keep getting a bit stronger, but it's on the low side for building muscle. Let's set your target at 100: that's your usual day plus a Greek yogurt at breakfast. Once 100 feels easy for two weeks, we'll step up to 110 and stop there. We'll look at your lifts again in four weeks.

data.said: 110 is still a stretch. Is 90 enough? I am getting a bit stronger.
data.checkin: Slept 7.5 h · Energy 68 · Soreness: light · Stress: medium · Readiness: green
data.food: Logs most days. Four-week average: 90 g protein (target 110, hit on 6 of 28 days), about 1,950 kcal, at maintenance. Breakfast is the lightest meal, about 10 g protein. Likes Greek yogurt, eggs, chicken thighs and lentil soup.
data.follow: Nov 25: she couldn't reach 120 g and asked for 46 g. The head coach's call was to lower her target to 110 g and raise it slowly if she doesn't see gains. Four weeks on: average about 90 g, 110 hit on 6 days of 28, weight unchanged at 150, squat up from 115 × 8 to 120 × 8, dumbbell press flat. The lower target helped a little but she still misses it most days.

program.heading: Week 1 of 4, as Kedge built it
program.athlete: Sam, 29. Lifting 2 years, wants strength and size, full gym, 4 days a week, about 60 minutes, nothing hurts. Squat 245 × 5, bench 185 × 5, deadlift 295 × 5.
days: Back squat 4 × 5 at effort 7–8; Romanian deadlift 3 × 8; walking lunge 3 × 10 each leg; leg curl 3 × 12; plank 3 × 40 s
Bench press 4 × 5; barbell row 4 × 8; overhead press 3 × 8; lat pulldown 3 × 10; curl 2 × 12
Deadlift 3 × 5; front squat 3 × 6; Bulgarian split squat 3 × 8; leg press 2 × 12; calf raise 3 × 12
Overhead press 4 × 5; weighted pull-up 4 × 6; incline dumbbell press 3 × 10; cable row 3 × 10; lateral raise 3 × 15; triceps pushdown 2 × 12
program.note: Weeks 2 and 3 add weight when every set reaches the top at the target effort. Week 4 is a lighter week.
